section_title: How will God free His people from those who trap them with lies?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 17 Now, O son of man, set your face against the daughters of your people who prophesy out of their own imagination. Prophesy against them 18 and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: Woe to the women who sew magic charms on their wrists and make veils for the heads of people of every height, in order to ensnare their souls. Will you ensnare the souls of My people but preserve your own? 19 You have profaned Me among My people for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread. By lying to My people who would listen, you have killed those who should not have died and spared those who should not have lived.

20 Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: See, I am against the magic charms with which you ensnare souls like birds, and I will tear them from your arms. So I will free the souls you have ensnared like birds. 21 I will also tear off your veils and deliver My people from your hands, so that they will no longer be prey in your hands. Then you will know that I am the LORD. 22 Because you have disheartened the righteous with your lies, even though I have caused them no grief, and because you have encouraged the wicked not to turn from their evil ways to save their lives, 23 therefore you will no longer see false visions or practice divination. I will deliver My people from your hands. Then you will know that I am the LORD.”

context_lines: The warning turns to women who likewise prophesy from their own imagination. The BSB describes wrist charms and veils used to ensnare people, with barley and scraps of bread involved in their trade.
The Lord charges them with profaning Him and reversing the response people need. Their lies dishearten the righteous and encourage the wicked to continue in ways that lead to death.
He declares that He will tear away the charms and veils and free the people caught like birds. Those being hunted will no longer be prey in these women’s hands.
The promise is both an end to false visions and a rescue of the people harmed by them. God does not simply expose the deception; He acts against the grip it has on His people.
common_interpretation_lines: The objects are understood differently. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/13.htm) and [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/13.htm), commenting on older wording about pillows and head coverings, emphasize the false ease and promised success being offered. Wesley treats the pillows as a figure for security.

The [Cambridge commentary on verses 18–20](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/ezekiel/13.htm) reads the bands and coverings as actual objects used in divination, and the [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/ezekiel/13) likewise understand them as amulets and veils associated with claims about life and death. That reading is reflected in the BSB’s wording about magic charms.

Both approaches recognize the harm stated at the end: the righteous are discouraged and the wicked are kept from turning back. The precise ritual details remain difficult, but the promise of deliverance from these lies is plain.
god_plan_lines: [John 8:31–36](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/8.htm) connects continuing in Jesus’ word with knowing the truth and being set free. Jesus explains the deeper slavery as slavery to sin, and identifies the Son as the One who brings true freedom.

John is not explicitly interpreting the charms in Ezekiel. The shared theme is God’s rescue from a bondage that false confidence cannot break. Ezekiel promises release from those who trap people with lies; Jesus explains the freedom He gives and calls His hearers to remain in His word.
